title: Ozonolysis of an alkene
subtitle: Ozone cuts a C=C bond; dimethyl sulfide gives two ketones

reactants.caption: 1,2-dimethylcyclopentene + ozone
reactants.learnerPrompt: Ozone adds across the C=C bond.
hintTiers: Ozone is a 1,3-dipole: its two end oxygens can both bond. With an alkene it makes a five-membered ring in one step (a [3+2] cycloaddition).

The O⁻ lone pair bonds to one alkene carbon, the C=C π pair bonds the other alkene carbon to the far end oxygen, and the O=O π pair moves onto the central oxygen, which loses its positive charge. Three arrows.
O⁻ lone pair → new bond to one alkene carbon; C=C π bond → new bond from the other alkene carbon to the other end oxygen; O=O π bond → a lone pair on the central oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The central oxygen carries the positive charge but has no room for a new bond. The ends of the dipole bond to the alkene.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Both new bonds are there, but the far end oxygen would have ten electrons. Move the O=O π pair onto the central oxygen.

molozonide.caption: the primary ozonide (molozonide, a 1,2,3-trioxolane)
molozonide.learnerPrompt: The primary ozonide falls apart (a retro-[3+2]).
hintTiers: The O–O–O ring is very weak. It splits into two pieces in the reverse of a cycloaddition, but along different bonds.
Break the C–C bond and one O–O bond: an oxygen lone pair forms C=O⁺, the C–C pair forms a C=O on the other carbon, and the O–O pair goes onto the middle oxygen. Three arrows.

Lone pair of one ring oxygen bonded to carbon → π bond to that carbon; the C–C bond → π bond between the other carbon and its oxygen; the O–O bond next to that oxygen → a lone pair on the middle oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Breaking a C–O bond just gives back ozone and the alkene. Break the C–C bond and an O–O bond instead.
The O–O pair should end on the middle oxygen, which becomes the O⁻ of the carbonyl oxide.

carbonyl-oxide.caption: a ketone and a carbonyl oxide (the Criegee intermediate) in one chain
carbonyl-oxide.learnerPrompt: The two ends of the chain recombine.
hintTiers: The carbonyl oxide is a new 1,3-dipole, and the ketone at the other end of the chain is its dipolarophile.
The O⁻ lone pair bonds to the ketone carbon, the ketone's C=O π pair bonds its oxygen to the carbonyl oxide carbon, and the C=O⁺ π pair goes onto that oxygen. Three arrows.
O⁻ lone pair → new bond to the ketone carbon; ketone C=O π bond → new bond from its oxygen to the carbonyl oxide carbon; C=O⁺ π bond → a lone pair on its oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That closes a three-membered dioxirane ring, a known side reaction of carbonyl oxides. Here the ketone at the other end of the chain is the partner: bond the O⁻ to the ketone carbon.

ozonide-and-sulfide.caption: the ozonide + dimethyl sulfide
hintTiers: Sulfur is a soft nucleophile, and the O–O bond is weak: the peroxide oxygen is the electrophile.
The sulfur lone pair bonds to one peroxide oxygen, and the O–O bond breaks onto the other. Two arrows.
Sulfur lone pair → new bond to one peroxide oxygen; the O–O bond → a lone pair on the other peroxide oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The ozonide carbons are crowded and carry no leaving group. The weak O–O bond is the target: attack an oxygen of the peroxide.
The oxygen bridging the two carbons is an ether oxygen. Attack one of the two oxygens joined to each other.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: sulfur bonds to a peroxide oxygen. Which bond breaks to make room?

sulfonium.caption: an alkoxide and an alkoxysulfonium ion in one ring
sulfonium.learnerPrompt: The ring falls apart into two ketones and dimethyl sulfoxide.
hintTiers: The alkoxide is a strong push, and dimethyl sulfoxide is a good leaving group. A three-arrow fragmentation through the bridging oxygen.
The O⁻ lone pair forms C=O, the bond from that carbon to the bridging oxygen becomes a C=O π bond to the other carbon, and the C–O bond to the sulfonium oxygen breaks onto it. Three arrows.

O⁻ lone pair → π bond to its carbon; that carbon's bond to the bridging oxygen → π bond between the bridging oxygen and the other carbon; that carbon's bond to the O–S oxygen → a lone pair on that oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Breaking the O–S bond would just give the sulfide back. The C–O bond breaks: the oxygen leaves with sulfur as dimethyl sulfoxide.

steps.explanationAfterStep: A concerted [3+2] cycloaddition (a 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition): both C–O bonds form on the same face of the alkene. Electron-rich, highly substituted alkenes such as this one react fastest.

The primary ozonide splits into a ketone and a carbonyl oxide, the Criegee intermediate. Because the alkene was in a ring, the two pieces stay joined by a chain. The ring is symmetrical, so splitting the other way gives the same pair.
A second [3+2] cycloaddition, with the C=O as the partner, gives the secondary ozonide. It has one O–O bond and an oxygen bridging the two carbons.

steps.caption: Dimethyl sulfide is added at −78 °C and the solution is warmed: a reductive work-up.

steps.explanationAfterStep: Sulfur attacks the weak O–O bond. Without a reducing agent the peroxide would oxidise the products further (an oxidative work-up with H₂O₂ gives carboxylic acids from aldehydes).
Both carbons become ketones and the sulfur leaves as dimethyl sulfoxide. The C=C bond has been cut in two: a cyclopentene becomes a 1,5-diketone.

mechanismSummary: Ozonolysis follows Criegee's mechanism. Ozone adds to the alkene in a [3+2] cycloaddition, giving the unstable primary ozonide. It splits in a retro-[3+2] into a ketone and a carbonyl oxide, which recombine in a second [3+2] to the secondary ozonide. Dimethyl sulfide reduces the O–O bond, and the ring fragments to two ketones and dimethyl sulfoxide. Here 1,2-dimethylcyclopentene stands in for ring A of Johnson's tetracycle: the same tetrasubstituted alkene in a five-membered ring with a methyl group on it (the B, C and D rings take no part and are left off). Cutting it turns the cyclopentene into a 1,5-diketone, ready to close a six-membered ring by an aldol.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 34 (1,3-dipolar cycloadditions: ozonolysis)
Criegee, Angewandte Chemie International Edition 1975, 14, 745 (the mechanism of ozonolysis)
Johnson, Gravestock and McCarry, Journal of the American Chemical Society 1971, 93, 4332 (acetylenic bond participation in biogenetic-like olefinic cyclisations: dl-progesterone)
